cells.tense: You see what matters here, and you're standing in it, not arguing with it.
cells.ask: Name the one thing that just became clear, say it plainly, then say what it means.
cells.core:
You can sit in a room where the next thing isn't obvious yet and have a sense of it anyway. Then it turns out right. You catch what matters before the reasons show up, and you've stopped needing the reasons to show up first. That's a steadier way to move through the unclear than working at it.

What's worth putting next to that: when something you see turns out useful, write down what you saw and when. Not to prove anything to anybody — just so you can look back later and find you were reading the room right the whole time. Let the record catch up to what you already had.

cells.tense: You're bracing for every turn the road might take, and there are far too many turns to hold.
cells.ask: Pick one question you're worried about and give it a deadline this week, then go with whatever you've got.
cells.core:
You're waiting for the moment you finally have enough to be sure. So you keep gathering — another angle, another piece, another way to look at it — and the gathering has quietly become the waiting. Nothing gets decided, because deciding while you're still short feels like guessing.

But you're trying to see the whole road before you take the first step, and the whole road isn't going to show up. What's getting buried under all that information is the thing you already half-know. Pick one question, put a date on it, and go with what you have when the date comes. Not knowing yet is not the emergency you're treating it as.

cells.tense: You stopped trusting what you saw back there, and you've been asking other people to see it for you since.
cells.ask: Say the next small thing you already believe, out loud, before asking anyone what they think.
cells.core:
Something you saw turned out to be right, and instead of making it easier to trust yourself, it seems to have made it harder. So now you take it out for a second opinion. You ask what someone else thinks before you admit you already had a view — and your view doesn't get to count until it does.

You can still see. You've just stopped going first. Start with something small. Say what you actually think before you check it against anyone, and let that be enough for today. Whatever it is you're trying to get back hasn't gone anywhere. It's been waiting for you to speak first.

cells.tense: You're steering yourself right now, and you're calling the steering something else.
cells.ask: Catch one decision this week you'd have called random, and name the hunch that was really behind it.
cells.core:
You keep arriving at the right call and calling it luck. You took the left turn and it worked out, and the story you tell is that you guessed. But you didn't guess — some part of you saw the shape of the thing and moved on it, and then you filed the move under something else.

That isn't a problem until you're trying to work out how you actually decide things, and then it's maddening, because half your best decisions are ones you don't think you made. Catch one this week and put your name on it. Not to congratulate yourself — just to know who's been steering.

The sentence that serves me more than them was a draft line about the veil becoming a wall; cut, because the card's vocabulary is not the person's.
